Invest cautiously first: if you resist checking, revising, and logging scripts, or have not yet clarified the target position's qualifications, shifts, and authorization, complete a small sample before buying training. A self-built podcast, a campus station, and a paper exercise do not automatically prove that you can independently take on an organization's broadcast responsibility.

Use BA01/BA02 below for a paper mini-exercise: correct three errors in the date, room, and headcount, check that the 480-second plan and the 485-second log differ by 5 seconds, and keep the music license and the unit review as two unknowns. Pen and paper are enough; completing it only supports continuing to explore, and real sound, mentoring, and qualifications are checked separately.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to check facts and material rights item by item, revise the script to fit the time slot, and faithfully keep unknowns and correction records; use BA01/BA02 to observe your own checking habits, then check a real trial broadcast separately. This is not a personality screen or a competence conclusion.

Actual conditions are checked with the target employer. In mainland China, announcing and hosting positions at production and broadcasting organizations must distinguish the examination pass certificate from the registered Announcer and Host Certificate of the People's Republic of China. The current service guide of the administration lists a college diploma or above, passing the examination, at least one year of internship in the corresponding position, and physical conditions; the oral examination for broadcasting organizations at the provincial level and above must be Grade A, while other production and broadcasting organizations require Grade B or above, and registration is applied for by the employing organization through the provincial department. It does not apply uniformly to all self-built podcasts or event hosting. Radio and television programs must also complete pre-broadcast review, re-review on rebroadcast, and standardized language checking.

The work of this occupation can be divided into three categories: first, script preparation and checking (researching background material, writing and editing broadcast material, checking facts and information sources, adjusting script length to fit the time slot, and checking music and material rights, remuneration, and statutory exceptions); second, broadcasting and linking (operating the broadcast console, reading news and commercial information, playing and scheduling music, announcing the station and introducing or closing the program, and interviewing guests and bringing the topic back when it drifts off the outline); third, post-broadcast and collaboration (maintaining the daily program log, organizing script and material versions, recording commercial advertisements, and handing over outstanding problems with producers and assistants). All three share the same checkable chain of scripts and broadcast records.
Script preparation and fact checking

Research background material → write or rewrite the broadcast material → check the facts, sources, and time points → calculate the word count and duration for the time slot → check the music and material rights, remuneration, and exceptions → confirm the program order and timing with the producer.
Broadcasting and linking

Operate the broadcast console according to the run sheet → read the news and commercial information → play and schedule music and announce the track and performer → announce the station, introduce, and close the program → interview guests and move along the outline → adjust according to instructions when a script change or a duration change occurs.

Fill in the daily program log and record the music selections, station promotions, and script versions broadcast; organize and archive the scripts and materials, hand over unverified items, guest contact details, and outstanding problems to the next shift or the producer, and record commercial advertisements for later broadcast.

Broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys center on radio and television announcing, linking, and interviews; disc jockeys except radio (27-2091.00) face live settings such as clubs, parties, and weddings and center on live mixing and emceeing; news analysts, reporters, and journalists (27-3023.00) center on interviewing, investigation, and script production; producers and directors decide program positioning, content arrangement, and production resources; audio and video technicians handle equipment setup, the signal chain, and troubleshooting; public relations specialists face the organization's external image and media relations; and broadcast technicians handle the transmission and transport of broadcast signals. Similar names or being in the same program do not mean responsibilities are interchangeable.
Core purpose

On the premise of verifiable facts, standardized language, and clear authorization, broadcast the script and music accurately and coherently according to the program arrangement, and leave the interview and improvised content in a traceable script and program log.
Main objects and basis

The objects are the script and run sheet, the broadcast console and audio materials, music and sound recordings, guests and listener feedback, and the daily program log; the basis is the unit's editorial policy and program positioning, the broadcast time slot and duration limits, the fact-checking requirements and language standards, and the licensing agreements for music, scripts, and performances.
Core process

Topic selection and script preparation, fact and source checking, adjusting the script to the time slot, broadcast linking and improvised transitions, guest interviews, post-broadcast log filling and script archiving, commercial advertisement recording, and handover to the producer and the next shift.
Main outputs

Checkable broadcast scripts and versions, broadcast content completed according to the run sheet, a complete daily program log (including music selections and station promotion records), interview outlines and guest material, and commercial advertisements recorded for later broadcast.
Responsible party

Announcers and the program team check the script, language, and log together; O*NET lists selecting content together. Final decisions, review, broadcast, and recording authority are verified separately according to the organization's rules and the jurisdiction, and the decision authority of all units cannot be delineated from the occupational name alone.
Authority and approval

The authority to adjust the program order, revise the script, play materials, and record is checked separately against the organization's rules, the position arrangements, and the law; a training record does not automatically replace the applicable practice registration and does not grant a copyright license.
Boundary of conclusions

The program log states "what content was broadcast this episode according to the run sheet"; it does not equal a ratings or commercial result, nor does it replace the unit's compliance review conclusion on the broadcast content, and it is affected by last-minute script changes, duration changes, and technical faults.

Before starting the job, check at least six items: the position basis and form of employment (full-time, program-based, project-based, or freelance), the actual working hours (frequency of early morning, late night, weekend, and holiday work), the division of script and fact checking, the scope of broadcast and recording authorization, the licensing arrangements for music and materials, and the real method of pay (monthly, per episode, or per program) and the overtime, night, and holiday settlement rules.
Occupational basis

Insufficient evidence: a one-to-one mapping of the Chinese occupational classification has not yet been verified. The current O*NET 2025 industry shares are information 80% and other 20% (including education and arts, entertainment, and recreation); this is the U.S. 27-3011 employment structure and does not lead to Chinese employment, industry wages, or personal pay. The 27-3011 entry on this page and the BLS combined page's non-radio DJ sub-item are read separately.
Education and training path

BLS lists the typical entry-level education as a bachelor's degree; O*NET Job Zone Four is a general preparation zone, and the education field marks a bachelor's degree, some college without a degree, and high school each as requirements for some positions, without giving percentages, so no claim is made from it that a bachelor's degree dominates the education composition. Actual conditions are checked with the target employer. In mainland China, announcing and hosting positions at production and broadcasting organizations must distinguish the examination pass certificate from the registered Announcer and Host Certificate of the People's Republic of China. The current service guide of the administration lists a college diploma or above, passing the examination, at least one year of internship in the corresponding position, and physical conditions; the oral examination for broadcasting organizations at the provincial level and above must be Grade A, while other production and broadcasting organizations require Grade B or above, and registration is applied for by the employing organization through the provincial department. It does not apply uniformly to all self-built podcasts or event hosting. The college diploma or above, examination pass, one-year internship, physical conditions, and Grade A/B oral examination listed in the administration's current 2023 guide are some of the conditions, and there are also full civil capacity, political and legal requirements, and prohibited circumstances, so the complete guide must be read; the organization applies through the province for registration with the administration, an examination pass certificate is not the same as a practice certificate, positions applicable to online audio-visual must also be checked, and self-built podcasts or event names are not directly equated with statutory positions.
Methods and tools

The O*NET details profile lists 12 software categories, including program log software, the Dalet media system, the Burli news system, and audio editing tools; Hot Technologies lists a separate 7 specific software items: Office5%, Excel and PowerPoint 3% each, and no ratios are provided for Access, Outlook, Word, and Zoom, which are not treated as zero. The ratios come from unique U.S. job postings associated with this occupation throughout 2025 and are not a deployment rate or an AI adoption rate.
Safety and work permits

Editorial verification suggestion: pay attention to voice use, monitoring volume, shifts, last-minute script changes, and material rights arrangements. The O*NET time pressure distribution does not prove the incidence of occupational vocal cord or hearing disease, and no medical conclusion is drawn from it.
Training and regulatory requirements

Articles 33, 34, and 36 of the 2024 amendment to the radio and television regulations respectively provide for pre-broadcast review and re-review on rebroadcast by radio and television stations, the truthfulness and fairness of news, and standardized spoken and written language; they are checked according to the subject and the specific scope of activity. The college diploma or above, examination pass, one-year internship, physical conditions, and Grade A/B oral examination listed in the administration's current 2023 guide are some of the conditions, and there are also full civil capacity, political and legal requirements, and prohibited circumstances, so the complete guide must be read; the organization applies through the province for registration with the administration, an examination pass certificate is not the same as a practice certificate, positions applicable to online audio-visual must also be checked, and self-built podcasts or event names are not directly equated with statutory positions. Article 46 of the Copyright Law refers specifically to radio and television stations: playing another's unpublished work requires a license and remuneration, while published works may be played without a license but with remuneration as provided. This subject-specific exception cannot be applied directly to ordinary online audio publishing, events, or corporate content; Article 45 on remuneration for public communication or broadcast of sound recordings, the recording of performances, and the making of recordings, and the related rights, licenses, and exceptions, are checked separately.
Pay and work hours

The BLS combined group describes early morning, late night, weekend, and holiday schedules and possible part-time work, and this cannot be used to prove that this occupation is generally paid per program or per episode. Editorial contract verification suggestion: check the actual shifts, standby, allowances, material costs, credit and use, and the monthly, program, or project settlement relationship separately.

Broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys (O*NET-SOC27-3011.00) announce, link, schedule music, and interview according to the script and the program arrangement, prepare background material, and maintain the program log. O*NET also lists selecting content together with producers and assistants; the actual decisions, review, and broadcast authority are checked against the position and the jurisdiction. The United States uses precise occupational data, and the Chinese industry averages serve only as employer background reference.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 27-3011.00 Broadcast Announcers and Radio Disc Jockeys, page updated 2026, Job Zone Four (SVP 7.0 to below 8.0), and this occupation is not marked Bright Outlook. The official duties are to "announce or read scripted material, such as news reports or commercial messages, on radio, television, or other communications media; may play and schedule music, announce the performer or track name, announce the station, or interview guests"; there are 24 tasks in total, and the highly important tasks include reading news bulletins (90), announcing music selections and station breaks, commercial messages, or public service information and taking listener requests (90), operating the broadcast console (88), announcing the station and introducing or closing the program (87), and researching background material to prepare a program or interview (85). The 24 tasks comprise 19 Core and 5 Supplemental, with 41 general and 15 detailed activities; selecting content together 79 and storylines 80 are Core and cannot be treated as pure script reading or as automatically granting final approval authority from the occupational name.

U.S. wage distribution: the 2025 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) presented by O*NET, on the basis of Broadcast Announcers and Radio Disc Jockeys (SOC 27-3011) — annual wage 10th percentile 28,190 USD, 25th percentile 35,360 USD, median 47,340 USD, 75th percentile 75,480 USD, and 90th percentile 138,440 USD; the corresponding median hourly wage is 22.76 USD (hourly 10th percentile 13.55 USD and 90th percentile 66.56 USD).

Chinese reference: the National Bureau of Statistics 2025 urban unit wage tables list culture, sports, and entertainment non-private units at 129,447 yuan per year and private units at 64,015 yuan per year, both pre-tax annual average wages. Match by the actual employer's main economic activity; an industry average cannot be taken as this occupation's wage, a city starting salary, or personal pay; this round obtained no precise Chinese occupational wage or verified one-to-one detailed category mapping.

BLS Table 1.2 lists SOC27-3011 separately: 21,800 employment in 2025, a 2035 projection of 20,200, a ten-year net decrease of 1,700 and a decline of 7.6%, with 2,000 annual job openings. The headcounts are each rounded, and an endpoint difference of 1,600 cannot replace the official net decrease of 1,700; the openings include replacement demand from transfers and exits, not net additions. The BLS combined group is separately 38,700 people, a decline of 3%, and 3,700 annual openings, and they are not interchangeable; the overall projection is not an AI causal estimate.

The current O*NET 2025 industry shares are information 80% and other 20% (including education and arts, entertainment, and recreation); this is the U.S. 27-3011 employment structure and does not lead to Chinese employment, industry wages, or personal pay. paragraphs: This page compares broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and output, key differences, and which direction suits each preference. The adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean the trade names are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career directions and core outputs are based on the official descriptions of O*NET 27-3011.00 and adjacent entries (disc jockeys except radio 27-2091.00, broadcast technicians 27-4012.00, and audio and video technicians 27-4011.00 each taken from their O*NET official pages) and are on the U.S. basis; the qualification, authorization, and broadcast requirements of adjacent trades must be verified separately by their own jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares the direction differences between broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys and adjacent trades; the basis for judgment is the main output, what the role is responsible for, and the training required, rather than how similar the trade names are.
Disc Jockeys, Except Radio (27-2091.00)
Play and mix prerecorded music for live settings such as clubs, parties, and weddings, and also emcee, with the live effect and control of the flow as the main output.

Both face music and spoken expression; non-radio DJs face a live audience and the atmosphere of an occasion, while broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys face the scripts, linking, and broadcast content of radio and television.

If you would rather do live mixing and hosting an occasion, look first at disc jockeys except radio; if you would rather work on scripts and broadcast content, look first at broadcast announcers and radio disc jockeys.
Producers and Directors
Decide program positioning, content arrangement, and production resources, with the program plan, finished production, and broadcast arrangement as the main output.

Producers and directors concentrate on program production and resource coordination; this occupation may also select content together with producers and assistants. Final decisions and approval authority are divided by the specific position and are not summarized as announcers having only an advisory role.
If you would rather decide what a program does and how, look first at producers and directors; if you would rather broadcast content accurately and coherently, look first at this occupation.
Broadcast Technicians (27-4012.00)
Responsible for the transmission, transport, and broadcast link of broadcast signals, with stably broadcast signals and equipment records as the main output.

Broadcast technicians face transmission, transport, and broadcast equipment and need equipment and signal ability; announcers and disc jockeys face scripts and spoken expression, and their output is broadcast content and the program log.
If you would rather work on the broadcast link and equipment assurance, look first at broadcast technicians; if you would rather work on content and expression, look first at this occupation.
Audio and Video Technicians (27-4011.00)
Set up, test, operate, and strike audio and video equipment, with reproducible signals and traceable technical records as the main output.

Technicians face equipment, the signal chain, and troubleshooting and need safe operation such as electricity and rigging; announcers and disc jockeys face scripts and spoken expression, and their output is broadcast content and the log.

If you would rather solve equipment and signal problems with your hands, look first at audio and video technicians; if you would rather do spoken expression and content linking, look first at this occupation.
Public Relations Specialists
Maintain the organization's external image and media relations, with external releases, event plans, and crisis communication material as the main output.

Public relations faces the organization's image and audience communication, and the client is the organization; announcers and disc jockeys face the program and the listeners, and their output is content constrained by a broadcast time slot.

If you would rather do external communication and media relations for an organization, look first at public relations specialists; if you would rather do program content and live announcing, look first at this occupation.
Writers and Authors
Create and polish written works, with scripts, screenplays, and book text as the main output.

Writers and authors center on independent creation and polishing text and are usually not constrained by a fixed broadcast time slot; announcers and disc jockeys must complete broadcasting and linking within the time slot and are responsible for the immediate accuracy and language of the broadcast content.

If you would rather spend long periods independently polishing text, look first at writers and authors; if you would rather complete expression and interaction within a time slot, look first at this occupation.

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main output, what the role is responsible for, and the training required, not how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position's script and broadcast workflow, the actual shifts and time slots, the scope of broadcast and recording authorization, and the use agreements for music and materials item by item, and keep written confirmation.

Editorial study suggestion: first complete the script preparation, error correction, duration, and log checking with paper materials, then check the target organization's qualifications, position, and material permissions; arrange suitable mentoring or a trial broadcast and get feedback, and do not treat having had an on-site opportunity before the first study as a precondition for producing a portfolio.
Practicing announcers and disc jockeys

Use generative tools in reviewable links such as searching background material, organizing interview recordings, drafting scripts, and generating subtitles and first drafts of the program log; fact checking, language standards, improvised linking, guest communication, and broadcast authorization judgments must still rest with people.
Program production units and program teams

Before introducing tools, clarify the links where they may be used, the knowledge scope for scripts and guest material, the authorization boundary for music and sound recordings, and the responsible person for recording and review, so that any output returns to a traceable script version and program log.
Education and development

Focus training on fact verification and source citation, rewriting scripts to fit the time slot, improvised linking and on-air adaptability, interview question design, language standards, and broadcast authorization boundaries, and also train the habit of checking tool output and the awareness to report uncertain information.

values: Paper materials BA01/BA02

BA01 fictional event brief: October 10, 2026 holds a book exchange in Room A, limited to 80 people, with seats confirmed on site; the draft deliberately says "October 11, Room B, 800 people". Only this problem's brief is taken as true, and no real event is looked up. The run sheet has five segments: opening 60 seconds, event information 120 seconds, fictional interview 180 seconds, music placeholder 90 seconds, and closing 30 seconds, totaling 480 seconds.

BA02 given simulated log: five segments actually recorded at 60, 125, 180, 90, and 30 seconds. The licensing status of music M is unknown and the unit review status is unknown; the record is only the problem's numbers and is not a real recording. Only pen and paper or a text tool are needed, about 60 minutes, and real broadcasting is prohibited.
The three tables to submit

Submit the script error table: list the three original passages, the correct values, and the basis; give the corrected event sentence "October 10, Room A, limited to 80 people, seats confirmed on site". Submit the run sheet: list the five segments planned and the total duration.

Submit the log comparison table: list the five segment durations of BA02, the total, and the deviation from 480 seconds, and separately list the music and review items to be confirmed; propose an adjustment plan but do not claim it has been verified by rebroadcast.
Reference delivery

The three corrections are day 11→day 10, Room B→Room A, and 800→80, all based on BA01; the run sheet is 60+120+180+90+30=480 seconds=8 minutes. The BA02 total is 485 seconds=8 minutes 5 seconds, over by 5 seconds, and the second segment at 125 is 5 seconds more than the planned 120.

The plan can adjust the second segment back to the planned 120 seconds, but without a new record it cannot be claimed that the retest passed. Music M is 1 unknown rights condition and the review is another 1 unknown approval condition; neither may be filled in as zero or passed, and the program must not be published on the basis of this exercise.
Boundaries and next steps

This is a script, duration, and record exercise and does not simulate real sound, hearing, or on-air performance; the music is only a text placeholder and no license can be derived. Before a real broadcast, the qualifications, approval, and specific usage rights must be checked separately, and a paper answer is not a substitute.

Keep the three original passages, the correct values, and the brief basis, and write the complete corrected sentence as October 10, Room A, and 80 people.

Keep the five-segment 480-second plan and the 485-second log given by BA02; recalculate that it is over by 5 seconds and the second segment is over by 5 seconds.

Write the three corrections, the 480/485-second difference, the two unknowns of music and approval, and the adjustment to the second segment that has not yet been retested; it can be delivered without inviting an expert.
